entries.324bad7964d6905ccc4af7a17b5e27e5ba3212f3: <div sID="gen10619" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Ps.17" sID="Ps.17"/> <div eID="gen10619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10620" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10621" type="x-p"/> David being in great distress and danger by the malice of his enemies, does, in this psalm, by prayer address himself to God, his tried refuge, and seeks shelter in him. I. He appeals to God concerning his integrity, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He prays to God still to be upheld in his integrity and preserved from the malice of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.5-Ps.17.8">ver. 5-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">13</reference>. III. He gives a character of his enemies, using that as a plea with God for his preservation, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.9-Ps.17.12">ver. 9-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">14</reference>. IV. He comforts himself with the hopes of his future happiness, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">ver. 15</reference>. Some make him, in this, a type of Christ, who was perfectly innocent, and yet was hated and persecuted, but, like David, committed himself and his cause to him that judgeth righteously.
entries.d509036dbc372d38014b0656cef55b3ef899cc16: <div eID="gen10621" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10620" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sincere and Importunate Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen10622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear the right, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , attend unto my cry, give ear unto my prayer, <hi type="italic">that goeth</hi> not out of feigned lips. <hi type="super">2</hi> Let my sentence come forth from thy presence; let thine eyes behold the things that are equal. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou hast proved mine heart; thou hast visited <hi type="italic">me</hi> in the night; thou hast tried me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> shalt find nothing; I am purposed <hi type="italic">that</hi> my mouth shall not transgress. 4 Concerning the works of men, by the word of thy lips I have kept <hi type="italic">me from</hi> the paths of the destroyer. <hi type="super">5</hi> Hold up my goings in thy paths, <hi type="italic">that</hi> my footsteps slip not. 6 I have called upon thee, for thou wilt hear me, O God: incline thine ear unto me, <hi type="italic">and hear</hi> my speech. <hi type="super">7</hi> show thy marvellous lovingkindness, O thou that savest by thy right hand them which put their trust <hi type="italic">in thee</hi> from those that rise up <hi type="italic">against them.</hi> <div eID="gen10622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10623" type="x-p"/> This psalm is a prayer. As there is a time to weep and a time to rejoice, so there is a time for praise and a time for prayer. David was now persecuted, probably by Saul, who hunted him like a partridge on the mountains; without were fightings, within were fears, and both urged him as a suppliant to the throne of mercy. He addresses himself to God in these verses both by way of appeal (<hi type="italic">Hear the right, O Lord!</hi> let my righteous cause have a hearing before thy tribunal, and give judgment upon it) and by way of petition (<hi type="italic">Give ear unto my prayer</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1">v. 1</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">v. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Incline thy ear unto me and hear my speech</hi>); not that God needs to be thus pressed with our importunity, but he gives us leave thus to express our earnest desire of his gracious answers to our prayers. These things he pleads with God for audience, 1. That he was sincere, and did not dissemble with God in his prayer: <hi type="italic">It goeth not out of feigned lips.</hi> He meant as he spoke, and the feelings of his mind agreed with the expressions of his mouth. Feigned prayers are fruitless; but, if our hearts lead our prayers, God will meet them with his favour. 2. That he had been used to pray at other times, and it was not his distress and danger that now first brought him to his duty: "<hi type="italic">I have called upon thee</hi> formerly (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">v. 6</reference>); therefore, Lord, hear me now." It will be a great comfort to us if trouble, when it comes, find the wheels of prayer a-going, for then we may come with the more boldness to the throne of grace. Tradesmen are willing to oblige those that have been long their customers. 3. That he was encouraged by his faith to expect God would take notice of his prayers: "I know <hi type="italic">thou wilt hear me,</hi> and therefore, O God, <hi type="italic">incline thy ear to me.</hi>" Our believing dependence upon God is a good plea to enforce our desires towards him. Let us now see, <div eID="gen10623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10624" type="x-p"/> I. What his appeal is; and here observe, <div eID="gen10624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10625" type="x-p"/> 1. What the court is to the cognizance and determination of which he makes his appeal; it is the court of heaven. "Lord, do thou hear the right, for Saul is so passionate, so prejudiced, that he will not hear it. Lord, <hi type="italic">let my sentence come forth from thy presence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.2">v. 2</reference>. Men sentence me to be pursued and cut off as an evil-doer. Lord, I appeal from them to thee." This he did in a public remonstrance before Saul's face (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12">1 Sam. xxiv. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord judge between me and thee</hi>), and he repeats it here in his private devotions. Note, (1.) The equity and extent of God's government and judgment are a very great support to injured innocency. If we are blackened, and abused, and misrepresented, by unrighteous men, it is a comfort that we have a righteous God to go to, who will take our part, who is the patron of the oppressed, whose judgment is according to truth, by the discoveries of which every person and every cause will appear in a true light, stripped of all false colours, and by the decisions of which all unrighteous dooms will be reversed, and to every man will be rendered according to his work. (2.) Sincerity dreads no scrutiny, no, not that of God himself, according to the tenour of the covenant of grace: <hi type="italic">Let thy eyes behold the things that are equal.</hi> God's omniscience is as much the joy of the upright as it is the terror of hypocrites, and is particularly comfortable to those who are falsely accused and in any wise have wrong done them. <div eID="gen10625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10626" type="x-p"/> 2. What the evidence is by which he hopes to make good his appeal; it is the trial God had made of him (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast proved my heart.</hi> God's sentence is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> right, because he always proceeds upon his knowledge, which is more certain and infallible than that which men attain to by the closest views and the strictest investigations. <div eID="gen10626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> (1.) He knew God had tried him, [1.] By his own conscience, which is God's deputy in the soul. <hi type="italic">The spirit of a man is the candle of the Lord,</hi> with this God had searched him, and <hi type="italic">visited him in the night,</hi> when he <hi type="italic">communed with his own heart upon his bed.</hi> He had submitted to the search, and had seriously reviewed the actions of his life, to discover what was amiss, but could find nothing of that which his enemies charged him with. [2.] By providence. God had tried him by the fair opportunity he had, once and again, to kill Saul; he had tried him by the malice of Saul, the treachery of his friends, and the many provocations that were given him; so that, if he had been the man he was represented to be, it would have appeared; but, upon all these trials, there was nothing found against him, no proof at all of the things whereof they accused him. <div eID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10628" type="x-p"/> (2.) God tried his heart, and could witness to the integrity of that; but, for the further proof of his integrity, he himself takes notice of two things concerning which his conscience bore him record:—[1.] That he had a fixed resolution against all sins of the tongue: "<hi type="italic">I have purposed</hi> and fully determined, in the strength of God's grace, <hi type="italic">that my mouth shall not transgress.</hi>" He does not say, "I hope that it will not," or, "I wish that it may not," but, "I have fully purposed that it shall not:" with this bridle he kept his mouth, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>. Note, Constant resolution and watchfulness against sins of the tongue will be a good evidence of our integrity. <hi type="italic">If any offend not in word, the same is a perfect man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.2">Jam. iii. 2</reference>. He does not say, "My mouth never shall transgress" (for in many things we all offend), but, "I have purposed that it shall not;" and he that searches the heart knows whether the purpose be sincere. [2.] That he had been as careful to refrain from sinful actions as from sinful words (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Concerning the</hi> common <hi type="italic">works of men,</hi> the actions and affairs of human life, <hi type="italic">I have,</hi> by the direction of thy word, <hi type="italic">kept myself from the paths of the destroyer.</hi>" Some understand it particularly, that he had not been himself a destroyer of Saul, when it lay in his power, nor had he permitted others to be so, but said to Abishai, <hi type="italic">Destroy him not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.9">1 Sam. xxvi. 9</reference>. But it may be taken more generally; he kept himself from all evil works, and endeavoured, according to the duty of his place, to keep others from them too. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The ways of sin are paths of the destroyer, of the devil, whose name is <hi type="italic">Abaddon</hi> and <hi type="italic">Apollyon,</hi> a destroyer, who ruins souls by decoying them into the paths of sin. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It concerns us all to keep out of the paths of the destroyer; for, if we walk in those ways that lead to destruction, we must thank ourselves if destruction and misery be our portion at last. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is by the word of God, as our guide and rule, that we must keep out of the paths of the destroyer, by observing its directions and admonitions, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.9">Ps. cxix. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> If we carefully avoid all the paths of sin, it will be very comfortable in the reflection, when we are in trouble. If we <hi type="italic">keep ourselves, that the wicked one touch us not</hi> with his temptations (<reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1 John v. 18</reference>), we may hope he will not be able to touch us with his terrors. <div eID="gen10628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10629" type="x-p"/> II. What his petition is; it is, in short, this, That he might experience the good work of God in him, as an evidence of and qualification for the good will of God towards him: this is grace and peace from God the Father. 1. He prays for the work of God's grace in him (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hold up my going in thy paths.</hi> Lord, I have, by thy grace, kept myself from the paths of the destroyer; by the same grace let me be kept in thy paths; let me not only be restrained from doing that which is evil, but quickened to abound always in that which is good. Let my goings be held in thy paths, that I may not turn back from them nor turn aside out of them; let them be held up in thy paths, that I may not stumble and fall into sin, that I may not trifle and neglect my duty. Lord, as thou hast kept me hitherto, so keep me still." Those that are, through grace, going in God's paths, have need to pray, and do pray, that their goings may be held up in those paths; for we stand no longer than he is pleased to hold us, we go no further than he is pleased to lead us, bear us up, and carry us. David had been kept in the way of his duty hitherto, and yet he does not think that this would be his security for the future, and therefore prays, "Lord, still hold me up." Those that would proceed and persevere in the way of God must, by faith and prayer, fetch in daily fresh supplies of grace and strength from him. David was sensible that his way was slippery, that he himself was weak, and not so well fixed and furnished as he should be, that there were those who watched for his halting and would improve the least slip against him, and therefore he prays, "Lord, hold me up, that my foot slip not, that I may never say nor do any thing that looks either dishonest or distrustful of thee and thy providence and promise." 2. He prays for the tokens of God's favour to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.7">v. 7</reference>. Observe here, (1.) How he eyes God as the protector and Saviour of his people, so he calls him, and thence he takes his encouragement in prayer: <hi type="italic">O thou that savest by thy right hand</hi> (by thy own power, and needest not the agency of any other) <hi type="italic">those who put their trust in thee from those that rise up against them.</hi> It is the character of God's people that they trust in him; he is pleased to make them confidants, for his secret is with the righteous; and they make him their trust, for to him they commit themselves. Those that trust in God have many enemies, many that rise up against them and seek their ruin; but they have one friend that is able to deal with them all, and, if he be for them, no matter who is against them. He reckons it his honour to be their Saviour. His almighty power is engaged for them, and they have all found him ready to save them. The margin reads it, <hi type="italic">O thou that savest those who trust in thee from those that rise up against thy right hand.</hi> Those that are enemies to the saints are rebels against God and his right hand, and therefore, no doubt, he will, in due time, appear against them. (2.) What he expects and desires from God: <hi type="italic">Show thy marvellous loving-kindness.</hi> The word signifies, [1.] Distinguishing favours. "Set apart thy loving-kindnesses for me; put me not off with common mercies, but be gracious to me, <hi type="italic">as thou usest to do to those who love thy name.</hi>" [2.] Wonderful favours. "O make thy loving-kindness admirable! Lord, testify thy favour to me in such a way that I and others may wonder at it." God's loving-kindness is marvellous for the freeness and the fulness of it; in some instances it appears, in a special manner, marvellous (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.23">Ps. cxviii. 23</reference>), and it will certainly appear so in the salvation of the saints, when Christ shall come to be <hi type="italic">glorified in the saints and to be admired in all those that believe.</hi>
entries.22b1dace7668426d17a8e3d151723005722d0295: <div eID="gen10629" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for Protecting Mercy; Character of David's Enemies.</title> <div sID="gen10630" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings, <hi type="super">9</hi> From the wicked that oppress me, <hi type="italic">from</hi> my deadly enemies, <hi type="italic">who</hi> compass me about. <hi type="super">10</hi> They are inclosed in their own fat: with their mouth they speak proudly. <hi type="super">11</hi> They have now compassed us in our steps: they have set their eyes bowing down to the earth; <hi type="super">12</hi> Like as a lion <hi type="italic">that</hi> is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places. <hi type="super">13</hi> Arise, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , disappoint him, cast him down: deliver my soul from the wicked, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> thy sword: <hi type="super">14</hi> From men <hi type="italic">which are</hi> thy hand, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , from men of the world, <hi type="italic">which have</hi> their portion in <hi type="italic">this</hi> life, and whose belly thou fillest with thy hid <hi type="italic">treasure:</hi> they are full of children, and leave the rest of their <hi type="italic">substance</hi> to their babes. <hi type="super">15</hi> As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness. <div eID="gen10630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> We may observe, in these verses, <div eID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10632" type="x-p"/> I. What David prays for. Being compassed about with enemies that sought his life, he prays to God to preserve him safely through all their attempts against him, to the crown to which he was anointed. This prayer is both a prediction of the preservation of Christ through all the hardships and difficulties of his humiliation, to the glories and joys of his exalted state, and a pattern to Christians to commit the keeping of their souls to God, trusting him to <hi type="italic">preserve them to his heavenly kingdom.</hi> He prays, <div eID="gen10632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10633" type="x-p"/> 1. That he himself might be protected (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">v. 8</reference>): "Keep me safe, hide me close, where I may not be found, where I may not be come at. Deliver my soul, not only my mortal life from death, but my immortal spirit from sin." Those who put themselves under God's protection may in faith implore the benefit of it. <div eID="gen10633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10634" type="x-p"/> (1.) He prays that God would keep him, [1.] With as much care as a man keeps the apple of his eye with, which nature has wonderfully fenced and teaches us to guard. If we keep God's law as the <hi type="italic">apple of our eye</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.2">Prov. vii. 2</reference>), we may expect that God will so keep us; for it is said concerning his people that whoso <hi type="italic">touches them touches the apple of his eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.2.8">Zech. ii. 8</reference>. [2.] With as much tenderness as the hen gathers her young ones under her wings with; Christ uses the similitude, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Hide me under the shadow of thy wings,</hi> where I may be both safe and warm." Or, perhaps, it rather alludes to the wings of the cherubim shadowing the mercy-seat: "Let me be taken under the protection of that glorious grace which is peculiar to God's Israel." What David here prays for was performed to the Son of David, our Lord Jesus, of whom it is said (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>) that God hid <hi type="italic">him in the shadow of his hand,</hi> hid him <hi type="italic">as a polished shaft in his quiver.</hi> <div eID="gen10634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10635" type="x-p"/> (2.) David further prays, "Lord, keep me from the wicked, from men of the world," [1.] "From being, and doing, like them, from walking in their counsel, and standing in their way, and eating of their dainties." [2.] "From being destroyed and run down by them. Let them not have their will against me; let them not triumph over me." <div eID="gen10635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> 2. That all the designs of his enemies to bring his either into sin or into trouble might be defeated (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Arise, O Lord!</hi> appear for me, disappoint him, and cast him down in his own eyes by the disappointment." While Saul persecuted David, how often did he miss his prey, when he thought he had him sure! And how were Christ's enemies disappointed by his resurrection, who thought they had gained their point when they had put him to death! <div eID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> II. What he pleads for the encouraging of his own faith in these petitions, and his hope of speeding. He pleads, <div eID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10638" type="x-p"/> 1. The malice and wickedness of his enemies: "They are such as are not fit to be countenanced, such as, if I be not delivered from them by the special care of God himself, will be my ruin. Lord, see what wicked men those are that oppress me, and waste me, and run me down." (1.) "They are very spiteful and malicious; they are <hi type="italic">my deadly enemies,</hi> that thirst after my blood, my heart's blood—<hi type="italic">enemies against the soul,</hi>" so the word is. David's enemies did what they could to drive him to sin and drive him away from God; they bade him <hi type="italic">go serve other gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1 Sam. xxvi. 19</reference>), and therefore he had reason to pray against them. Note, Those are our worst enemies, and we ought so to account them, that are enemies to our souls. (2.) "They are very secure and sensual, insolent and haughty (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are enclosed in their own fat,</hi> wrap themselves, hug themselves, in their own honour, and power, and plenty, and then make light of God, and set his judgments at defiance, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Ps. lxxiii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.27">Job xv. 27</reference>. They wallow in pleasure, and promise themselves that to-morrow shall be as this day. And therefore with their mouth they speak proudly, glorying in themselves, blaspheming God, trampling upon his people, and insulting them." See <reference osisRef="Rev.13.5-Rev.13.6">Rev. xiii. 5, 6</reference>. "Lord, are not such men as these fit to be mortified and humbled, and made to know themselves? Will it not be for thy glory <hi type="italic">to look upon these proud men and abase them?</hi>" (3.) "They are restless and unwearied in their attempts against me: They <hi type="italic">compass me about,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.9">v. 9</reference>. They have now in a manner gained their point; they have surrounded us, they have compassed us in our steps, they track us wherever we go, follow us as close as the hound does the hare, and take all advantages against us, being both too many and too quick for us. And yet they pretend to look another way, and set their eyes bowing down to the earth, as if they were meditating, retired into themselves, and thinking of something else;" or (as some think), "They are watchful and intent upon it, to do us a mischief; they are down-looked, and never let slip any opportunity of compassing their design." (4.) "The ringleader of them (that was Saul) is in a special manner bloody and barbarous, politic and projecting (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">like a lion</hi> that lives by prey and is therefore greedy of it." It is as much the meat and drink of a wicked man to do mischief as it is of a good man to do good. He is like <hi type="italic">a young lion lurking in secret places,</hi> disguising his cruel designs. This is fitly applied to Saul, who sought David <hi type="italic">on the rocks of the wild goats</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.2">1 Sam. xxiv. 2</reference>) and in <hi type="italic">the wilderness of Ziph</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.2">Ps. xxvi. 2</reference>), where lions used to lurk for their prey. <div eID="gen10638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10639" type="x-p"/> 2. The power God had over them, to control and restrain them. He pleads, (1.) "Lord, they are <hi type="italic">thy sword;</hi> and will any father suffer his sword to be drawn against his own children?" As this is a reason why we should patiently bear the injuries of men, that they are but the instruments of the trouble (it comes originally from God, to whose will we are bound to submit), so it is an encouragement to us to hope both that their wrath shall praise him and that the remainder thereof he will restrain, that they are God's sword, which he can manage as he pleases, which cannot move without him, and which he will sheathe when he has done his work with it. (2.) "They are <hi type="italic">thy hand,</hi> by which thou dost chastise thy people and make them feel thy displeasure." He therefore expects deliverance from God's hand because from God's hand the trouble came. <hi type="italic">Una eademque manus vulnus opemque tulit—The same hand wounds and heals.</hi> There is no flying from God's hand but by flying to it. It is very comfortable, when we are in fear of the power of man, to see it dependent upon and in subjection to the power of God; see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6-Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 6, 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">15</reference>. <div eID="gen10639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10640" type="x-p"/> 3. Their outward prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">v. 14</reference>): "Lord, appear against them, for," (1.) "They are entirely devoted to the world, and care not for thee and thy favour. They are <hi type="italic">men of the world,</hi> actuated by the spirit of the world, walking according to the course of this world, in love with the wealth and pleasure of this world, eager in the pursuits of it (making them their business) and at ease in the enjoyments of it—making them their bliss. They <hi type="italic">have their portion in this life;</hi> they look upon the good things of this world as the best things, and sufficient to make them happy, and they choose them accordingly, place their felicity in them, and aim at them as their chief good; they rest satisfied with them, their souls take their ease in them, and they look no further, nor are in any care to provide for another life. These things are their consolation (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.24">Luke vi. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">their good things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">their reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.5">Matt. vi. 5</reference>), the penny they agreed for, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.13">Matt. xx. 13</reference>. Now, Lord, shall men of this character be supported and countenanced against those who honour thee by preferring thy favour before all the wealth in this world, and taking thee for their portion?" <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Ps. xvi. 5</reference>. (2.) They have abundance of the world. [1.] They have enlarged appetites, and a great deal wherewith to satisfy them: <hi type="italic">Their bellies thou fillest with thy hidden treasures.</hi> The things of this world are called <hi type="italic">treasures,</hi> because they are so accounted; otherwise, to a soul, and in comparison with eternal blessings, they are but trash. They are hidden in the several parts of the creation, and hidden in the sovereign disposals of Providence. They are God's hidden treasures, for the earth is his and the fulness thereof, though the men of the world think it is their own and forget God's property in it. Those that fare deliciously every day have their <hi type="italic">bellies filled with these hidden treasures;</hi> and they will but <hi type="italic">fill the belly</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1 Cor. vi. 13</reference>); they will not fill the soul; they are not bread for that, nor can they satisfy, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. They are husks, and ashes, and wind; and yet most men, having no care for their souls, but all for their bellies, take up with them. [2.] They have numerous families, and a great deal to leave to them: <hi type="italic">They are full of children,</hi> and yet their pasture is not overstocked; they have enough for them all, and <hi type="italic">leave the rest of their substance to their babes,</hi> to their grand-children; and this is their heaven, it is their bliss, it is their all. "Lord," said David, "<hi type="italic">deliver me from them;</hi> let me not have my portion with them. Deliver me from their designs against me; for, they having so much wealth and power, I am not able to deal with them unless the Lord be on my side." <div eID="gen10640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10641" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleads his own dependence upon God as his portion and happiness. "They have their portion in this life, but as for me (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">v. 15</reference>) I am none of them, I have but little of the world. <hi type="italic">Nec habeo, nec careo, nec curo—I neither have, nor need, nor care for it.</hi> It is the vision and fruition of God that I place my happiness in; that is it I hope for, and comfort myself with the hopes of, and thereby distinguish myself from those who have their portion in this life." Beholding God's face with satisfaction may be considered, (1.) As our duty and comfort in this world. We must in righteousness (clothed with Christ's righteousness, having a good heart and a good life) by faith behold God's face and set him always before us, must entertain ourselves from day to day with the contemplation of the beauty of the Lord; and, when we awake every morning, we must be satisfied with his likeness set before us in his word, and with his likeness stamped upon us by his renewing grace. Our experience of God's favour to us, and our conformity to him, should yield us more satisfaction than those have whose belly is filled with the delights of sense. 2. As our recompence and happiness in the other world. With the prospect of that he concluded the foregoing psalm, and so this. That happiness is prepared and designed only for the righteous that are justified and sanctified. They shall be put in possession of it when they awake, when the soul awakes, at death, out of its slumber in the body, and when the body awakes, at the resurrection, out of its slumber in the grave. That blessedness will consist in three things:—[1.] The immediate vision of God and his glory: <hi type="italic">I shall behold thy face,</hi> not, as in this world, through a glass darkly. The knowledge of God will there be perfected and the enlarged intellect filled with it. [2.] The participation of his likeness. Our holiness will there be perfect. This results from the former (<reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1 John iii. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.</hi> [3.] A complete and full satisfaction resulting from all this: <hi type="italic">I shall be satisfied,</hi> abundantly satisfied with it. There is no satisfaction for a soul but in God, and in his face and likeness, his good-will towards us and his good work in us; and even that satisfaction will not be perfect till we come to heaven.  <chapter eID="Ps.17"/> <div eID="gen10641" type="x-p"/>

entries.4462f50d6c1e5d0126af381a14437add186934c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5598"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 17</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15">Psa 17:1-15</reference>. This Psalm is termed a prayer because the language of petition is predominant. With a just cause, sincerely presented, the writer prays for a just decision and help and protection. Pleading former mercies as a ground of hope, he urges his prayer in view of the malice, pride, rapacity, and selfishness of his foes, whose character is contrasted with his pious devotion and delight in God's favor.</title> <div sID="gen8520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5598"/><hi type="bold">2. sentence--</hi>acquitting judgment.<div eID="gen8520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from thy presence--</hi>Thy tribunal.<div eID="gen8521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things that are equal--</hi>just and right, do Thou regard. <div eID="gen8522" type="x-p"/>
entries.c41281a1c8463f341aab6ffcee13b8ad81fec041: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5599"/><div sID="gen8523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5599"/><hi type="bold">3. proved ... visited ... tried--</hi>His character was most rigidly tested, at all times, and by all methods, affliction and others (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>).<div eID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purposed that, &c.--</hi>or, my mouth does not exceed my purpose; I am sincere. <div eID="gen8524" type="x-p"/>
entries.68b6624d21763cf3ad0d199195ff2ff8cb2d9b63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5600"/><div sID="gen8525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5600"/><hi type="bold">4. works of men--</hi>sinful practices.<div eID="gen8525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the word of thy lips--</hi>as a guide (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.9">Psa 119:9</reference>, 11, 95).<div eID="gen8526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroyer--</hi>violent man. <div eID="gen8527" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdd747b9c3971caa359a1da8db22d841ab0c9f5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5601"/><div sID="gen8528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5601"/>5. May be read as an assertion "my steps or goings have held on to Thy paths." <div eID="gen8528" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe7baae0a26d0de80164d24b6f3744e1429d852d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5602"/><div sID="gen8529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5602"/><hi type="bold">6. wilt hear me--</hi>that is, graciously (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.4">Psa 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen8529" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cd793812a5868416b568dc3fa306ba168a0adf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5603"/><div sID="gen8530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5603"/><hi type="bold">7. Show--</hi>set apart as special and eminent (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.18">Ex 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen8530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy right hand--</hi>for Thy power. <div eID="gen8531" type="x-p"/>
entries.55fa9b560e4502dcf02bec9b1927565aa98f7b12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5604"/><div sID="gen8532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5604"/>8. Similar figures, denoting the preciousness of God's people in His sight, in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">De 32:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mt 23:37</reference>. <div eID="gen8532" type="x-p"/>
entries.690451d00eb931b30d8fa86273345c31ba91b882: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5605"/><div sID="gen8533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5605"/><hi type="bold">9. compass me--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.10-Ps.118.12">Psa 118:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen8533" type="x-p"/>
entries.def24114e258d6c38f99b7e8185c5805186a4309: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5606"/><div sID="gen8534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5606"/><hi type="bold">10. enclosed ... fat--</hi>are become proud in prosperity, and insolent to God (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Psa 73:7</reference>). <div eID="gen8534" type="x-p"/>
entries.93f75eadc24fae8614cdf7a29b3fece29817724c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5607"/><div sID="gen8535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5607"/>11. They pursue us as beasts tracking their prey. <div eID="gen8535" type="x-p"/>
entries.e065c08e6a8aac4c21d04f954d6d8d98ab0eebc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5608"/><div sID="gen8536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5608"/>12. The figure made more special by that of a lion lurking. <div eID="gen8536" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2ce31f065ebdf4e6dd810f00b7a50704b7beb37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5609"/><div sID="gen8537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5609"/><hi type="bold">13-15. disappoint--</hi>literally, "come before," or, "encounter him." Supply "with" before "sword" (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>), and "hand" (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>). These denote God's power. <div eID="gen8537" type="x-p"/>

entries.603cae08b805022ec038f79379979340d176c706: <div eID="gen18909" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18910" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18911" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18911" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18910" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18912" type="x-p"/> David implores the succor of God against his enemies; and professes his integrity and determination to live to God's glory, <reference osisRef="Psa.17.1">Psa 17:1</reference>. He prays for support, and expresses strong confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.17.5-Psa.17.9">Psa 17:5-9</reference>; describes the malice and cruelty of his enemies, and prays against them, <reference osisRef="Psa.17.10-Psa.17.14">Psa 17:10-14</reference>; receives a strong persuasion of support and final victory, <reference osisRef="Psa.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>. <div eID="gen18912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18913" type="x-p"/> The title is, A prayer of David; in which there is nothing that requires explanation. David was most probably the author of this Psalm; and it appears to have been written about the time in which Saul had carried his persecution against him to the highest pitch. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.12">1Sam 27:1-12</reference> : The Arabic calls it "A prayer of a perfect man, of Christ himself, or of any one redeemed by him." Dr. Delaney, in his life of David, supposes that this poem was written just after parting with Jonathan, when David went into exile. <div eID="gen18913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18914" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18915" type="x-p"/> Hear the right - Attend to the justice of my cause, יהוה צדק Yehovah tsedek, righteous Jehovah. "O righteous Jehovah, attend unto my cry." <div eID="gen18915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18916" type="x-p"/> Goeth not out of feigned lips - My supplication is sincere: and the desire of my heart accompanies the words of my lips.
entries.db48f183fcb6aaad1cc0ae95aeabb2803e195183: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18917" type="x-p"/> My sentence come forth from thy presence - Thou knowest my heart, and my ways; judge me as thou shalt find; let me not fall under the judgment of man. <div eID="gen18917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18918" type="x-p"/> Let thine eyes behold the things that are equal - Thou knowest whether I render to all their due, and whether others act justly by me. Thou canst not be deceived: do justice between me and my adversaries.
entries.284496a5934968e6e39e5060d0820686feae8557: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18919" type="x-p"/> Thou hast proved mine heart - Thou well knowest whether there be any evil way in me. Thou hast given me to see many and sore trials; and yet, through thy mercy, I have preserved my integrity both to thee and to my king. Thou hast seen me in my most secret retirements, and knowest whether I have plotted mischief against him who now wishes to take away my life. <div eID="gen18919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18920" type="x-p"/> Thou hast tried me - צרפתני tseraphtani; Thou hast put me to the test, as they do metals in order to detect their alloy, and to purify them: well expressed by the Vulgate, Igne me examinasti, "Thou hast tried me by fire;" and well paraphrased in my old Psalter, - The examynd me the lykkenyng of the fournas, that purges metal, and imang al this, wykednes es nout funden in me: that es, I am funden clene of syn, and so ryghtwis. - He who is saved from his sin is right wise; he has found the true wisdom. <div eID="gen18920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18921" type="x-p"/> My mouth shall not transgress - This clause is added to the following verse by the Vulgate and Septuagint: "That my mouth may not speak according to the works of men, I have observed difficult ways because of the words of thy lips." That is, So far from doing any improper action, I have even refrained from all words that might be counted inflammatory or seditious by my adversaries; for I took thy word for the regulation of my conduct, and prescribed to myself the most painful duties, in order that I might, in every respect, avoid what would give offense either to thee or to man. Among the genuine followers of God, plots and civil broils are never found.
entries.1426ba480f75371031425019a10b8007e6d863ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18922" type="x-p"/> The paths of the destroyer - Some render, hard or difficult paths, the sense of which is given above. But the passage is exceedingly obscure. My old Psalter translates and paraphrases as follows: - <div eID="gen18922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18923" type="x-p"/> Trans. That my mouthe speke noght the werkes of men, for the wordes of thi lippes I haf keped hard wayse. <div eID="gen18923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18924" type="x-p"/> Par - That es, that nothing passe of my mouthe bot at falles to the louyng of the; noght til werkes of men, that dos o gaynes thy wil; als to say, I spak noght bot gude; and for the wordes of thi lippes, that es, to ful fil the wordes that thi prophetes saide; I kepe hard waies of verteus and of tribulacioun, the qwilk men thynk hard; and for thi thai leve the hard way til heven, and takes the soft way til hel; but it es ful hard at the end.
entries.f90616b6a01162637efaf9b27368b7543aacd8ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18925" type="x-p"/> Hold up my goings in thy paths - David walked in God's ways; but, without Divine assistance, he could not walk steadily, even in them. The words of God's lips had shown him the steps he was to take, and he implores the strength of God's grace to enable him to walk in those steps. He had been kept from the paths of the destroyer; but this was not sufficient; he must walk in God's paths - must spend his life in obedience to the Divine will. Negative holiness ean save no man. "Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire."
entries.45a34cdf4ef91209b285a2e8bb4defc9e045edd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18926" type="x-p"/> Incline thine ear unto me - David prayed from a conviction that God would hear: but he could not be satisfied unless he received an answer. In a believer's mind the petition and the answer should not be separated.
entries.540a83619e9c62bb2d62c646f9fecc607bad1faa: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18927" type="x-p"/> Show thy marvellous lovingkindness - David was now exposed to imminent danger; common interpositions of Providence could not save him; if God did not work miracles for him, he must fall by the hand of Saul. Yet he lays no claim to such miraculous interpositions; he expects all from God's lovingkindness. <div eID="gen18927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18928" type="x-p"/> The common reading here is הפלה חסדיך haphleh chasadeycha, "distinguish thy holy ones;" but הפלא haple, "do wonders," is the reading of about seventy MSS., some ancient editions, with the Septuagint, Vulgate, Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic. The marginal reading of this verse is nearer the original than that of the text.
entries.d6948b3a2fcf62be45cbc36d769ea72bfc8823e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18929" type="x-p"/> Keep me as the apple of the eye - Or, as the black of the daughter of eye. Take as much care to preserve me now by Divine influence, as thou hast to preserve my eye by thy good providence. Thou hast entrenched it deeply in the skull; hast ramparted it with the forehead and cheek-bones; defended it by the eyebrow, eyelids, and eyelashes; and placed it in that situation where the hands can best protect it. <div eID="gen18929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18930" type="x-p"/> Hide me under the shadow of thy wings - This is a metaphor taken from the hen and her chickens. See it explained at large in the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.23.37">Mat 23:37</reference> (note). The Lord says of his followers, <reference osisRef="Zac.2.8">Zac 2:8</reference> : "He that toucheth you, toucheth the apple of mine eye." How dear are our eyes to us! how dear must his followers be to God!
entries.8b214dfe84f0e122eef9a15e93852f27a0e47ea5: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18931" type="x-p"/> From my deadly enemies, who compass me about - This is a metaphor taken from huntsmen, who spread themselves around a large track of forest, driving in the deer from every part of the circumference, till they are forced into the nets or traps which they have set for them in some particular narrow passage. The metaphor is carried on in the following verses.
entries.cecfe9a72d148bd6d16b408b63792c5ec916c548: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18932" type="x-p"/> They are enclosed in their own fat - Dr. Kennicott, Bishop Horsley, Houbigant, and others, read the passage thus: עלי חבלמו סגרו alai chablamo sageru, "They have closed their net upon me." This continues the metaphor which was introduced in the preceding verse, and which is continued in the two following: and requires only that עלי ali, "upon me," should began this verse instead of end the preceding; and that חלב cheleb, which signifies fat, should be read חבל chebel, which signifies rope, cable, or net. This important reading requires only the interchange of two letters. The Syriac translates it, shut their mouth: but the above emendation is most likely to be true. <div eID="gen18932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18933" type="x-p"/> They speak proudly - Having compassed the mountain on which I had taken refuge, they now exult, being assured that they will soon be in possession of their prey.
entries.f3f10bcfe50f257e6f0a58e6bb18c7feb1c90c5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18934" type="x-p"/> They have now compassed us in our steps - Instead of אשרנו ashshurenu, "our steps," Dr. Kennicott and others recommend אשרינו ashreynu, "O lucky we, at last we have compassed him." He cannot now escape; he is sure to fall into our hands. <div eID="gen18934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18935" type="x-p"/> They have set their eyes bowing down to the earth - All the commentators and critics have missed the very expressive and elegant metaphor contained in this clause. Kennicott says, They drove the hart into toils, and then shot him. Bishop Horsley says, on the clause, They have set their eyes bowing down to the earth: "This is the attitude of huntsmen, taking aim at an animal upon the ground." No, it is the attitude of the huntsmen looking for the slot, or track of the hart's, hind's, or antelope's foot on the ground. See at the conclusion of the Psalm.
entries.9489f9b26aaeb4fa36e71d1b7b7d91608f999cc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18936" type="x-p"/> Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey - I believe the word lion is here used to express Saul in his strength, kingly power and fierce rapacity. See the observations at the end of the Psalm.
entries.cbed8c667b4b692f865fd672a591ad845000713c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen18936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18937" type="x-p"/> Arise, O Lord, disappoint him - When he arises to spring upon and tear me to pieces, arise thou, O Lord; disappoint him of his prey; seize him, and cast him down. <div eID="gen18937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18938" type="x-p"/> Deliver my soul - Save my life. <div eID="gen18938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18939" type="x-p"/> From the wicked, which is thy sword - Saul is still meant, and we may understand the words as either implying the sword, the civil power, with which God had intrusted him, and which he was now grievously abusing; or, it may mean, deliver me by Thy sword - cut him off who wishes to cut me off. On this ground the next verse should be read from men, By thy hand. So the margin. The hand of God not only meaning his power, but his providence.
entries.a9e2b24b5de68bd47e98585e34ff3f9ded5b6c36: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen18939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18940" type="x-p"/> From men of the world, which have - ממתים מחלד mimethim mecheled, from mortal men of time; temporizers; men who shift with the times, who have no fixed principle but one, that of securing their own secular interest: and this agrees with what follows - which have their portion in this life; who never seek after any thing spiritual; who have bartered heaven for earth, and have got the portion they desired; for thou fillest their belly with thy hid treasure. Their belly - their sensual appetites - is their god; and, when their animal desires are satisfied, they take their rest without consideration, like the beasts that perish. <div eID="gen18940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18941" type="x-p"/> Their portion in this life - בחיים bachaiyim, in lives, probably meaning heritable lands and estates; for they leave them to their children, they descend to posterity, and every one has his life portion in them. They are lands of lives. <div eID="gen18941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18942" type="x-p"/> They are full of children - Have a numerous offspring, whom they educate in the same principles, and to whom they leave a large earthly patrimony, and who spend it as their fathers have done, and perhaps even more dissolutely. Often covetous fathers lay up riches, which profligate sons scatter to all the winds of heaven. I have seen many instances of this.
entries.474b974ea5425b8725d99ae7d2e6840f0f42b68f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen18942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18943" type="x-p"/> As for me - I cannot be satisfied with such a portion. <div eID="gen18943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18944" type="x-p"/> I will behold thy face - Nothing but an evidence of thy approbation can content my soul. <div eID="gen18944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18945" type="x-p"/> In righteousness - I cannot have thy approbation unless I am conformed to thy will. I must be righteous in order that my heart and life may please thee. <div eID="gen18945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18946" type="x-p"/> I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness - Nothing but God can satisfy the wishes of an immortal spirit. He made it with infinite capacities and desires; and he alone, the infinite Good, can meet and gratify these desires, and fill this all-capacious mind. No soul was ever satisfied but by God; and he satisfies the soul only by restoring it to his image, which, by the fall, it has lost. <div eID="gen18946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18947" type="x-p"/> I think there is an allusion here to the creation of Adam. When God breathed into him the breath of lives, and he became a living soul, he would appear as one suddenly awaked from sleep. The first object that met his eyes was his glorious Creator, and being made in his image and in his likeness, he could converse with him face to face - was capable of the most intimate union with him, because he was filled with holiness and moral perfection. Thus was he satisfied, the God of infinite perfection and purity filling all the powers and faculties of his soul. David sees this in the light of the Divine Spirit, and knows that his happiness depends on being restored to this image and likeness; and he longs for the time when he shall completely arise out of the sleep and death of sin, and be created anew after the image of God, in righteousness and true holiness. I do not think that he refers to the resurrection of the body, but to the resurrection of the soul in this life; to the regaining the image which Adam lost. <div eID="gen18947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18948" type="x-p"/> The paraphrase in my old Psalter understands the whole of this Psalm as referring to the persecution, passion, death, and resurrection of Christ; and so did several of the primitive fathers, particularly St. Jerome and St. Augustine. I shall give a specimen from <reference osisRef="Psa.17.11">Psa 17:11</reference> : - <div eID="gen18948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18949" type="x-p"/> Projicientes me, nunc circumdederunt me: oculos suos statuerunt declinare in terram. <div eID="gen18949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18950" type="x-p"/> Trans. Forth castand me now, thai haf umgyfen me: thair egheu thai sette to heelde in the erde. <div eID="gen18950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18951" type="x-p"/> Par - Forth kasten me out of the cite, als the stede had bene fyled of me: now thai haf umgyfen me in the cros hyngand, als folk that gedyrs til a somer gamen: for thai sett thair eghen, that es the entent of thaire hert to heeld in the erde; that es, in erdly thynges to covayte tham, and haf tham. And thai wende qwen thai slew Crist that he had suffird al the ill, and thai nane. <div eID="gen18951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18952" type="x-p"/> Perhaps some of my readers may think that this needs translating, so far does our present differ fronn our ancient tongue. <div eID="gen18952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18953" type="x-p"/> Text - They have now cast me forth; they have surrounded me: their eyes they set down to the earth. <div eID="gen18953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18954" type="x-p"/> Par - They have cast me out of the city, as if the state were to be defiled by me: now they have surrounded me hanging on the cross, as people gathered together at summer games. For they set their eyes, that is, the intent of their heart, down to the earth; that is, earthly things, to covet them and to have them: and they thought, when they slew Christ, that he had suffered all the ill, and they none. <div eID="gen18954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18955" type="x-p"/> By the slot or track of the hart on the ground, referred to in <reference osisRef="Psa.17.11">Psa 17:11</reference>, experienced huntsmen can discern whether there have been a hart there, whether he has been there lately, whether the slot they see be the track of a hart or a hind, and whether the animal be young or old. All these can be discerned by the slot. And if the reader have that scarce book at hand, Tuberville on Hunting, 4th, 1575 or 1611, he mill find all this information in chapter 22, p. 63, entitled, The Judgment and Knowledge by the Slot of a Hart; and on the same page; a wood-cut, representing a huntsman with his eyes set, bowing down to the earth, examining three slots which he had just found. The cut is a fine illustration of this clause. Saul and his men were hunting David, and curiously searching every place to find out any track, mark, or footstep, by which they might learn whether he had been in such a place, and whether he had been there lately. Nothing can more fully display the accuracy and intensity of this search than the metaphor contained in the above clause. He who has been his late Majesty's huntsmen looking for the slot in Windsor Forest will see the strength and propriety of the figure used by the psalmist. <div eID="gen18955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18956" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18957" type="x-p"/> Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey - This is the picture of Saul. While his huntsmen were beating every bush, prying into every cave and crevice, and examining every foot of ground to find out a track, Saul is ready, whenever the game is started, to spring upon, seize, and destroy it. The metaphors are well connected, well sustained, and strongly expressive of the whole process of this persecution. <div eID="gen18957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18958" type="x-p"/> In the ninth verse the huntsmen beat the forest to raise and drive in the game. In the tenth they set their nets, and speak confidently of the expected success. In the eleventh, they felicitate themselves on having found the slot, the certain indication of the prey being at hand. And in the twelfth, the king of the sport is represented as just ready to spring upon the prey; or, as having his bow bent, and his arrow on the string, ready to let fly the moment the prey appears. It is worthy of remark, that kings and queens were frequently present, and were the chiefs of the sport; and it was they who, when he had been killed, broke up the deer: 1. Slitting down the brisket with their knife or sword; and, 2. Cutting off the head. And, as Tuberville published the first edition of his book in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, he gives a large wood-cut, p. 133, representing this princess just alighted from her horse - the stag stretched upon the ground - the huntsman kneeling, holding the fore foot of the animal with his left hand, and with his right presenting a knife to the queen for the purpose of the breaking up. As the second edition was published in the reign of James the First, the image of the queen is taken out and a whole length of James introduced in the place. <div eID="gen18958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18959" type="x-p"/> The same appears in Tuberville's Book of Falconrie, connected with the above. In p. 81, edition 1575, where the flight of the hawk at the heron is represented, the queen is seated on her charger: but in the edition of 1611 King James is placed on the same charger, the queen being removed. <div eID="gen18959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18960" type="x-p"/> The lion is the monarch of the forest; and is used successfully here to represent Saul, king of Israel, endeavoring to hunt down David; hernoming him in on every side; searching for his footsteps; and ready to spring upon him, shoot him with his bow, or pierce him with his javelin, as soon as he should be obliged to flee from his last cover. The whole is finely imagined, and beautifully described.  <chapter eID="Ps.17"/> <div eID="gen18960" type="x-p"/>

entries.e056f865ec610272ddb220e86ac6f04cac488502: <div eID="gen9189" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Flight of an innocent and Persecuted Man for Refuge in the Lord, Who Knoweth Them That Are His</title> <div sID="gen9190" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15">Psa 17:1-15</reference> is placed after <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference>, because just like the latter (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.11.7">Psa 11:7</reference>) it closes with the hope of a blessed and satisfying vision of God. In other respects also the two Psalms have many prominent features in common: as, for instance, the petition שׁמרני, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; the retrospect on nightly fellowship with God, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Psa 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>; the form of address in prayer אל, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">Psa 17:6</reference>; the verb תּמך, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>, etc. (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi> p. 49), notwithstanding a great dissimilarity in their tone. For <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference> is the first of those which we call Psalms written in the indignant style, in the series of the Davidic Psalms. The language of the Psalms of David, which is in other instances so flowing and clear, becomes more harsh and, in accordance with the subject and mood, as it were, full of unresolved dissonances (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.1">Psa 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.140.1">Psa 140:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.1">Psa 58:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Psa 36:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2-Ps.10.11">Psa 10:2-11</reference>) when describing the dissolute conduct of his enemies, and of the ungodly in general. The language is then more rough and unmanageable, and wanting in the clearness and transparency we find elsewhere. The tone of the language also becomes more dull and, as it were, a dull murmur. It rolls on like the rumble of distant thunder, by piling up the suffixes <hi type="italic">mo , āmo , ēmo</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.10">Psa 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.16">Psa 35:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.9">Psa 64:9</reference>, where David speaks of his enemies and describes them in a tone suggested by the indignation, which is working with his breast; or in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.12-Ps.59.14">Psa 59:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.10-Ps.21.13">Psa 21:10-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.140.10">Psa 140:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.7">Psa 58:7</reference>, where, as in prophetic language, he announces to them of the judgment of God. The more vehement and less orderly flow of the language which we find here, is the result of the inward tumult of his feelings. <div eID="gen9190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9191" type="x-p"/> There are so many parallels in the thought and expression of thought of this Psalm in other Davidic Psalms (among those we have already commented on we may instance more especially <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1">Psa 7:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference>, and also <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>), that even Hitzig admits the לדוד. The author of the Psalm is persecuted, and others with him; foes, among whom one, their leader, stands prominently forward, plot against his life, and have encompassed him about in the most threatening manner, eager for his death. All this corresponds, line for line, with the situation of David in the wilderness of <hi type="italic">Maon</hi> (about three hours and three quarters S.S.E. of Hebron), as narrated in 1Sa 23:25., when Saul and his men were so close upon the heels of David and his men, that he only escaped capture by a most fortunate incident. <div eID="gen9191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9192" type="x-p"/> The only name inscribed on this Psalm is תּפּלּה (a prayer), the most comprehensive name for the Psalms, and the oldest (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">Psa 72:20</reference>); for שׁיר and מזמור were only given to them when they were sung in the liturgy and with musical accompaniment. As the title of a Psalm it is found five times (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.1">Psa 17:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.1">Psa 86:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.92.1">Psa 92:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1">Psa 142:1</reference>) in the Psalter, and besides that once, in Hab. Habakkuk’s תפלה is a hymn composed for music. But in the Psalter we do not find any indication of the Psalms thus inscribed being arranged for music. The strophe schema is 4. 7; 4. 4. 6. 7.
entries.7900383eae670f07ef51d27961ed345cc7e402f3: <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.2">Psa 17:1-2</reference> צדק is the accusative of the object: the righteousness, intended by the suppliant, is his own (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference></hi>). He knows that he is not merely righteous in his relation to man, but also in his relation to God. In all such assertions of pious self-consciousness, that which is intended is a righteousness of life which has its ground in the righteousness of faith. True, Hupfeld is of opinion, that under the Old Testament nothing was known either of righteousness which is by faith or of a righteousness belonging to another and imputed. But if this were true, then Paul was in gross error and Christianity is built upon the sand. But the truth, that faith is the ultimate ground of righteousness, is expressed in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">Gen 15:6</reference>, and at other turning-points in the course of the history of redemption; and the truth, that the righteousness which avails before God is a gift of grace is, for instance, a thought distinctly marked out in the expression of Jeremiah צדקנוּ ה, “the Lord our righteousness.” The Old Testament conception, it is true, looks more to the phenomena than to the root of the matter (<hi type="italic">ist mehr phänomenell als wurzelhaft</hi>), is (so to speak) more Jacobic than Pauline; but the righteousness of life of the Old Testament and that of the New have one and the same basis, viz., in the grace of God, the Redeemer, towards sinful man, who in himself is altogether wanting in righteousness before God (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">Psa 143:2</reference>). Thus there is no self-righteousness, in David’s praying that the righteousness, which in him is persecuted and cries for help, may be heard. For, on the one hand, in his personal relation to Saul, he knows himself to be free from any ungrateful thoughts of usurpation, and on the other, in his personal relation to God free from מרמה, i.e., self-delusion and hypocrisy. The shrill cry for help, רנּה, which he raises, is such as may be heard and answered, because they are not lips of deceit with which he prays. The actual fact is manifest לפני יהוה, therefore may his right go forth מלּפניו, - just what does happen, by its being publicly proclaimed and openly maintained - from Him, for His eyes, the eyes of Him who knoweth the hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>), behold מישׁרים (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Psa 75:3</reference> = בּמישׁרים, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>, and many other passages), in uprightness, i.e., in accordance with the facts of the case and without partiality. מישׁרים might also be an accusative of the object (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.17">1Ch 29:17</reference>), but the usage of the language much more strongly favours the adverbial rendering, which is made still more natural by the confirmatory relation in which <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.17.2">Psa 17:2</reference></hi> stands to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.17.2">Psa 17:2</reference></hi>.
entries.b0fd3f29c21c535a55791221e4b0f2d74918d0e4: <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3-Ps.17.5">Psa 17:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen9192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9193" type="x-p"/> David refers to the divine testing and illumination of the inward parts, which he has experienced in himself, in support of his sincerity. The preterites in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference> express the divine acts that preceded the result בּל־תּמצא, viz., the testing He has instituted, which is referred to in צרפתּני and also בּחנתּ as a trying of gold by fire, and in פּקד as an investigation (<reference osisRef="Job.7.18">Job 7:18</reference>). The result of the close scrutiny to which God has subjected him in the night, when the bottom of a man’s heart is at once made manifest, whether it be in his thoughts when awake or in the dream and fancies of the sleeper, was and is this, that He does not find, viz., anything whatever to punish in him, anything that is separated as dross from the gold. To the mind of the New Testament believer with his deep, and as it were microscopically penetrating, insight into the depth of sin, such a confession concerning himself would be more difficult than to the mind of an Old Testament saint. For a separation and disunion of flesh and spirit, which was unknown in the same degree to the Old Testament, has been accomplished in the New Testament consciousness by the facts and operations of redemption revealed in the New Testament; although at the same time it must be remembered that in such confessions the Old Testament consciousness does not claim to be clear from sins, but only from a conscious love of sin, and from a self-love that is hostile to God. <div eID="gen9193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9194" type="x-p"/> With זמּותי David begins his confession of how Jahve found him to be, instead of finding anything punishable in him. This word is either an infinitive like חנּות (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.10">Psa 77:10</reference>) with the regular <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> accentuation, formed after the manner of the הל verbs, - in accordance with which Hitzig renders it: my thinking does not overstep my mouth, - or even <hi type="italic">1 pers. praet</hi>., which is properly <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, but does also occur as <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.32.41">Deu 32:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.16">Isa 44:16</reference> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference>), - according to which Böttcher translates: should I think anything evil, it dare not pass beyond my mouth, - or (since זמם may denote the determination that precedes the act, e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.4.28">Jer 4:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">Lam 2:17</reference>): I have determined my mouth shall not transgress. This last rendering is opposed by the fact, that עבר by itself in the ethical signification “to transgress” (cf. post-biblical עברה παράβασις) is not the usage of the biblical Hebrew, and that when יעבר־פּי stand close together, פי is presumptively the object. We therefore give the preference to Böttcher’s explanation, which renders זמותי as a hypothetical perfect and is favoured by <reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Pro 30:32</reference> (which is to be translated: and if thou thinkest evil, (lay) thy hand on thy mouth!). Nevertheless בל יעבר־פי is not the expression of a fact, but of a purpose, as the combination of בל with the future requires it to be taken. The psalmist is able to testify of himself that he so keeps evil thoughts in subjection within him, even when they may arise, that they do not pass beyond his mouth, much less that he should put them into action. But perhaps the psalmist wrote פּיך originally, “my reflecting does not go beyond Thy commandment” (according to Num 22:18; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.24">1Sa 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.29">Pro 8:29</reference>), - a meaning better suited, as a result of the search, to the nightly investigation. The ל of לפעלּות fo ל need not be the ל of reference (as to); it is that of the state or condition, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference>; Psa 69:22. אדם, as perhaps also in <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>; Hos 6:7 (if אדם is not there the name of the first man), means, men as they are by nature and habit. בּדבר שׂפתיך does not admit of being connected with לפעלּות: at the doings of the world contrary to Thy revealed will (Hofmann and others); for פּעל בּ cannot mean: to act contrary to any one, but only: to work upon any one, Job 35:6. These words must therefore be regarded as a closer definition, placed first, of the שׁמרתּי which follows: in connection with the doings of men, by virtue of the divine commandment, he has taken care of the paths of the oppressor, viz., not to go in them; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.21">1Sa 25:21</reference> is an instance in support of this rendering, where שׁמרתי, as in <reference osisRef="Job.2.6">Job 2:6</reference>, means: I have kept (Nabal’s possession), not seizing upon it myself. Jerome correctly translates <hi type="italic">vias latronis</hi>; for פּריץ signifies one who breaks in, i.e., one who does damage intentionally and by violence. The confession concerning himself is still continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>, for the <hi type="italic">inf. absol. </hi>תּמך, if taken as imperative would express a prayer for constancy, that is alien to the circumstances described. The perfect after בּל is also against such a rendering. It must therefore be taken as <hi type="italic">inf. historicus</hi>, and explained according to <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>, cf. Psa 41:13. The noun following the <hi type="italic">inf. absol.</hi>, which is usually the object, is the subject in this instance, as, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.40.2">Job 40:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.12">Pro 17:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.2">Ecc 4:2</reference>, and frequently. It is אשׁוּרי, and not אשּׁוּרי, אשׁור (a step) never having the שׁ dageshed, except in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.11">Psa 17:11</reference> and Job 31:7.
entries.5da476efb06d6d0d65aed574a83e4cf4a9e2257e: <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6-Ps.17.7">Psa 17:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen9194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9195" type="x-p"/> It is only now, after his inward parts and his walk have been laid open to Jahve, that he resumes his petition, which is so well justified and so soundly based, and enters into detail. The אני<note placement="foot">The word is pointed אני, in correct texts, as אני always is when it has <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> and <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> follows, e.g., also Psa 116:16. This <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> demands an emphatic intonation of the secondary word in its relation to the principal word (which here is קראתיך).</note> found beside קראתיך (the perfect referring to that which has just now been put into execution) is meant to imply: such an one as he has described himself to be according to the testimony of his conscience, may call upon God, for God hears such and will therefore also hear him. הט אזנך exactly corresponds to the Latin <hi type="italic">au-di</hi> (<hi type="italic">aus-cul-ta</hi>). The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הפלה (הפליא, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>) signifies here to work in an extraordinary and marvellous manner. The danger of him who thus prays is great, but the mercies of God, who is ready and able to help, are still greater. Oh that He may, then, exhibit all its fulness on his behalf. The form of the address resembles the Greek, which is so fond of participles. If it is translated as Luther translates it: “Show Thy marvellous lovingkindness, Thou Saviour of those who trust in Thee, Against those who so set themselves against Thy right hand,” then חוסים is used just as absolutely as in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">Pro 14:32</reference>, and the right hand of God is conceived of as that which arranges and makes firm. But “to rebel against God’s right (not <hi type="italic">statuta</hi>, but <hi type="italic">desteram</hi>)” is a strange expression. There are still two other constructions from which to choose, viz., “Thou Deliverer of those seeking protection from adversaries, with Thy right hand” (Hitz.), or: “Thou Helper of those seeking protection from adversaries, at Thy right hand” (Aben-Ezra, Tremell.). This last rendering is to be preferred to the two others. Since, on the one hand, one says מחסה מן, refuge from..., and on the other, חסה בּ to hide one’s self in any one, or in any place, this determining of the verbal notion by the preposition (on this, see above on <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Psa 2:12</reference>) must be possible in both directions. ממּתקוממים is equivalent to ממתקוממיהם <reference osisRef="Job.27.7">Job 27:7</reference>; and חוסים בימינך, those seeking protection at the strong hand of Jahve. The force of the ב is just the same as in connection with הסתּתּר,   1Sa 23:19. In Damascus and throughout Syria - Wetzstein observes on this passage - the weak make use of these words when they surrender themselves to the strong: Arab. <hi type="italic">anâ b - qabḍt ydk</hi>, “I am in the grasp of thy hand (in thy closed hand) i.e., I give myself up entirely to thee.”<note placement="foot">Cognate in meaning to חסה ב are Arab. <hi type="italic">'sttr b</hi> and <hi type="italic">tadarrâ b</hi>, e.g., Arab. <hi type="italic">tḏrrâ b - 'l - ḥâ'ṭ mn 'l - rı̂ḥ</hi> he shelters (hides) himself by the wall from the wind, or Arab. <hi type="italic">bâl‛ḍât mn 'l - brd</hi>, by a fire against the cold, and Arab. <hi type="italic">‛âḏ</hi>, which is often applied in like manner to God’s protection. Thus, e.g., (according to Bochâri’s <hi type="italic">Sunna</hi>) a woman, whom Muhammed wanted to seize, cried out: Arab. <hi type="italic">a‛ûḏu b - 'llh mnk</hi>, I place myself under God’s protection against thee, and he replied: Arab. <hi type="italic">‛uḏti bi - ma‛âḏin</hi>, thou hast taken refuge in an (inaccessible) <hi type="italic">asylum</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic">Job</hi>, i. 310 n. and ii. 22 n. 2).</note>
entries.cd394d2c0cd35cb1f967fe1fbce6fb0fdd73fb42: <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8-Ps.17.9">Psa 17:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen9195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9196" type="x-p"/> The covenant relationship towards Himself in which Jahve has placed David, and the relationship of love in which David stands to Jahve, fully justified the oppressed one in his extreme request. The apple of the eye, which is surrounded by the iris, is called אישׁון, the man (Arabic <hi type="italic">insân</hi>), or in the diminutive and endearing sense of the termination <hi type="italic">on</hi>: the little man of the eye, because a picture in miniature of one’s self is seen, as in a glass, when looking into another person’s eye. בּת־עין either because it is as if born out of the eye and the eye has, as it were, concentrated itself in it, or rather because the little image which is mirrored in it is, as it were, the little daughter of the eye (here and <reference osisRef="Lam.2.18">Lam 2:18</reference>). To the Latin <hi type="italic">pupilla </hi>(<hi type="italic">pupula</hi>), Greek κόρη, corresponds most closely בּבת עין, Zec 2:12, which does not signify the gate, aperture, sight, but, as בּת shows, the little boy, or more strictly, the little girl of the eye. It is singular that אישׁון here has the feminine בּת־עין as the expression in apposition to it. The construction might be genitival: “as the little man of the apple of the eye,” inasmuch as the saint knows himself to be so near to God, that, as it were, his image in miniature is mirrored in the great eye of God. But (1) the more ozdinary name for the pupil of the eye is not בּת עין, but אישׁון; and (2) with that construction the proper point of the comparison, that the apple of the eye is an object of the most careful self-preservation, is missed. There is, consequently, a combination of two names of the pupil or apple of the eye, the usual one and one more select, without reference to the gender of the former, in order to give greater definition and emphasis to the figure. The primary passage for this bold figure, which is the utterance of loving entreaty, is <reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">Deu 32:10</reference>, where the dazzling anthropomorphism is effaced by the lxx and other ancient versions;<note placement="foot">Vid., Geiger, <hi type="italic">Urschrift und Ueberstezungen der Bibel</hi>, S. 324.</note> cf. also Sir. 17:22. Then follows another figure, taken from the eagle, which hides its young under its wings, likewise from Deut 32, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.17.11">Psa 17:11</reference>, for the figure of the hen (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mat 23:37</reference>) is alien to the Old Testament.
